title: Drifters That Feed the Sea
question: What makes something plankton, and why does ocean life depend on them?
hook: A bacterium and a jellyfish share the same label, and it has nothing to do with their family tree.
idea: Plankton are defined by drifting with the currents rather than by ancestry, and together they form the base of the marine food web.

beats.prompt: Match each group of sea life to how it lives
pairs: Drifts, unable to swim against currents
Lives on the deep sea floor
Floats on or near the surface
beats.explain: These names sort sea life by where it lives and how well it moves, not by what kind of organism it is.

beats.prompt: Sort each drifter by how it gets its food
beats.explain: Phytoplankton such as diatoms and cyanobacteria make their own food, while zooplankton such as radiolarians and copepods eat other organisms.

beats.prompt: Trade winds carry dust from the Sahara out over the eastern Atlantic. What happens to the phytoplankton in those waters?

choices.label: They are abundant, fed by iron in the dust
They are sparse, smothered by the dust
choices.feedback: Dust sounds harmful, but it delivers iron, a nutrient phytoplankton need.

choices.label: They are sparse, since dry land nearby adds nothing
choices.feedback: It seems an arid coast should mean barren water, but the wind-borne dust is the supply.

choices.label: They are unaffected, since only light matters
choices.feedback: Light is the main driver, but nutrients such as iron also limit growth.

beats.explain: Iron mainly reaches the ocean as dust settling on the surface, so waters beside unproductive, arid land like the Sahara typically have abundant phytoplankton.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: The main cause of differences in plankton abundance is the availability of light.
Large areas of the tropical oceans receive abundant light.
Light is all phytoplankton need, so nothing else can hold them back there.
So those tropical waters should be among the most productive anywhere.
beats.explain: Nutrients are a second limit: tropical and subtropical waters with plenty of light still have relatively low production because nitrate, phosphate and silicate are limited.
